cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and the sense of what's fair is steady in you.
cells.act: count what the ending gave you
cells.ask: Something finished this year — a job, a habit, a way you used to be. Count what it gave you. Not a story, just the count. Nothing to fix.
cells.core: When something has run its course, you can sit with it and say what it was worth. Not in a ledger, in your gut. That's the shape when this is working: you don't rush past what ended, and you don't inflate it either. You let the thing have been what it was, and you take what it left. The patient wait is already behind you. What's left is the picking up, and the picking up is quiet work that most people skip. They turn an ending into a lesson or a complaint. You can let it be a yield. What you gather this way stays accurate, because you did the waiting that made it real, and nobody handed you the total.
cells.sheetLine: You know what something was worth, and you let it count.
cells.verb: keeping a private account of what's fair
cells.place: where you become what you are

cells.tense: You are bracing against a future where the scales might tip, so the weighing never stops.
cells.act: hold someone else up with what you have
cells.ask: Notice somebody carrying something heavy. Do one real thing for them — an errand, a meal, a straight answer — and call it done. Skip the scales after.
cells.core: When the sense of what's right runs ahead of you, it turns into arithmetic. Every exchange gets measured before it happens, and the measuring has no finish, because a future can't be settled in advance. So you hold back or push forward to force a balance that hasn't arrived. What gets lost is the plain help you're more than able to offer. Your strength is real. It just stays behind the calculation instead of reaching anyone. Fairness moves when you stop auditing it. Give one thing fully, let it land where it lands, and skip going back to weigh whether it was fair. The balance you're after sits on the far side of that help, not the near one.
cells.sheetLine: You weigh the fairness ahead until nothing gets to happen.
cells.verb: keeping a private account of what's fair
cells.place: where you become what you are

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you, holding a fairness that never got to settle.
cells.act: point to the passage you can see
cells.ask: Pick a route through something you already got through, and say it out loud to somebody still in the middle of it. Plainly. Don't walk it for them.
cells.core: The compass is in you, but it's pointed at something already done. You're checking an account from a time you can't go back to, and the checking has taken the place of the living. What you see is real — what should have been, what didn't get settled. It just hasn't been able to become anything here, because you're not here. Feeling your way back into the present isn't the move. Pointing is. Take something you already got through and hand the route to somebody still in it. That's a small act, and it puts what you carry to work. Practice returns by being used on something small enough to finish.
cells.sheetLine: You see the passage, but you've stopped pointing anyone to it.
cells.verb: keeping a private account of what's fair
cells.place: where you become what you are

cells.tense: You are writing this whole thing — the fairness, the count, the weight — and calling it nothing much.
cells.act: distinguish what is yours from what you borrowed
cells.ask: List what's pulling at you. Next to each one, mark whether it's actually yours to carry. Leave the list as it is when you're done — change nothing, just mark it.
cells.core: There's a read in you about what's fair that shows up as plain fact. You walk into a room and the weights become visible — what's owed, what isn't, who's carrying something that wasn't theirs to pick up. When you account for how you got that, you credit the situation. Anyone would notice, you say. But the reading is yours, and it's good, and the fact that it's quiet doesn't make it borrowed. Privacy is part of how it works. What's unclaimed is your name on it. Put your own mark on the read and the next one comes through clearer. You're not deciding anything here, just sorting whose weight is whose.
cells.sheetLine: You see what's fair here. You file it under circumstance.
cells.verb: keeping a private account of what's fair

The asks survive being wrong because each is a small act from the medicine's own list, done once, and useful even if the read of the seat is off. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that names their moral accounting as a wound rather than a capacity. So all four cells stay with what is felt and what can be done, and none diagnoses the person.
